claims.claim: Religion is a social institution: an organized and integrated set of beliefs, behaviors, and norms centered on basic social needs and values, and a cultural universal — some form of religion appears in every known culture, usually practiced publicly by a group.

Working definition: religion is a system of beliefs and practices oriented around the sacred; Durkheim (1915) called it a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, and OpenStax's glossary defines it as a system of beliefs, values, and practices concerning what a person holds sacred or spiritually significant.

Definitions of religion are debated: the OpenStax text notes people attach the word to very different things (a building, a practice, a concept that guides daily life), Durkheim himself offered multiple formulations, and the sacred-centered definition is a working definition rather than a settled one.

The elements of religion include beliefs (specific ideas members hold to be true), rituals (behaviors required or expected of members), community (the group that practices together — Durkheim's 'single moral community'), and symbols (objects or gestures carrying sacred meaning); sociologists also distinguish religious experience, the conviction of connection to the divine.

Durkheim's analysis credits religion with three societal functions: it binds people together (social cohesion), promotes behavior consistency (social control), and offers strength during life's transitions and tragedies (meaning and purpose).

Functionalist analysis extends the functions: religion provides answers to spiritual mysteries, offers emotional comfort in crisis, and creates opportunities for social interaction and group formation.

Sociologists describe four organizational types, without ranking them: church (the broad, established body of believers — Durkheim's word for the moral community), denomination (a large, mainstream religion not sponsored by the state), sect (a small, new offshoot of a denomination), and cult (a small, secretive, highly controlling group with a charismatic leader).

Durkheim's sacred–profane distinction: the sacred is extraordinary and set apart, the profane is ordinary life, and religion happens when society separates the two; the same object can shift between sacred and profane depending on the meaning it carries.

Weber's Protestant ethic argument (The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, 1905): certain Protestant teachings — work hard, succeed, and do not spend profits on frivolous things — helped fuel the development of capitalism; the thesis is one of the most important and controversial topics in the sociology of religion, and scholars continue to debate it.

Religion both unites and divides: it fosters group cohesion and integration, yet shared identity can harden into in-group versus out-group feeling, and religious disputes and persecution have fed conflicts, including wars and genocides, throughout history.

Sociology studies religion descriptively: it distinguishes the experience, beliefs, and rituals people share and applies its methods to understand religion's role in people's lives, rather than certifying or dismissing any religion's truth claims.

Scale: Pew Research Center estimated that 75.8 percent of the world's people identified with a religion as of 2020 (Christians 28.8%, Muslims 25.6%, religiously unaffiliated 24.2%, Hindus 14.9%, Buddhists 4.1%, Jews about 0.2%, other religions 2.2%).

positions: Durkheim's classic formulation centers on sacred things: religion is a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things (1915).
OpenStax's glossary broadens this to a system of beliefs, values, and practices concerning what a person holds sacred or spiritually significant.
Everyday usage attaches the word to very different things — places of worship, practices, concepts that guide daily life (OpenStax 15-introduction).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the Durkheim/OpenStax sacred-centered formulation as a working definition and explicitly notes that definitions are debated; no single definition is presented as final.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Weber's Protestant ethic thesis holds
positions: Weber (1905) argued that certain Protestant teachings encouraged hard work, success, and thrift, helping fuel the development of capitalism (OpenStax 15.1).
OpenStax reports the claim has been one of the most important and controversial topics in the sociology of religion, with scholars continuing to debate its applicability.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the thesis at one-line depth, attributed to Weber, and flags it as contested rather than settled fact.

positions: Religion fosters cohesion, meaning, and social order (Durkheim's functions, per OpenStax 15.1).
Religion also produces in-group versus out-group feeling and has been tied to persecution and conflict, including wars (OpenStax 15.1, 15.3, and the chapter introduction).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both faces as part of the record — religion unites and divides — attributing each claim to the source that supports it.

Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.
